headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Deep at the Jetty, Weakfish Waking at Ponquogue
subhead: A neap tide slowed the current down, but it didn't slow down the bite — you just have to fish the right three hours.
body_markdown:
By eleven o'clock last Tuesday I'd already made my call for the week: skip the day tide entirely, wait for the outgoing after midnight, and set up in the deep hole on the ocean side of the east jetty where the current pours through hardest. That's been the program all month, but it's especially true right now with the back bay running warm and the bass shoved into a strict low-light and after-dark pattern. Daytime, they're sulking somewhere cool. After dark, with the water dropping and the current ripping past the rocks, they come up to feed, and that's when you want to be standing there.

The first quarter neap landed today, which took some of the snap out of the current compared to the spring tide push we had a couple weeks back. I'll take it, honestly — a softer outgoing means the window at the jetty stretches longer instead of slamming shut in ninety minutes. I worked eels on a fish-finder rig in eighteen to twenty-two feet off the rocks starting about an hour before the tide turned, and connected on three fish in the 28 to 34 inch range between 1 and 3 a.m., all on the meat of the drop. A buddy fishing bucktails — the black-and-purple 2-ounce, slow-rolled along bottom — picked up a slot fish and lost a bigger one right at the rocks where the current seams up. Nothing epic, but three or four solid bass in a night session at the inlet this time of year is a night worth having, and it beats standing there empty in daylight heat.

We flagged this last week — said the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings — and that's exactly what's playing out at Ponquogue Bridge right now. Dusk into full dark, on the last two hours of the incoming, guys working small bucktails tipped with squid strips or 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Shrimp under the lights near the pilings have been finding weakfish in the 16 to 20 inch class consistently enough to call it a pattern, not a fluke catch. The key is fishing tight to the shadow line the bridge lights throw on the water — that's where the bait bunches up and the weakfish sit waiting. Don't overpower the retrieve. A slow lift-and-drop right on the edge of that light line has been the difference between a bent rod and nothing.

Daytime, the move in the bay is fluke, and it's been the most dependable thing going out here for weeks now. The flats off Tiana Beach and the drift lanes around Warner's Island and Cormorant Reef are holding fish in eight to fifteen feet, and moving water is doing the work — outgoing has been slightly better than incoming, probably because it's pulling bait off the flats into the channel edges where the fluke are stacked up waiting. Standard drift rig, 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow with the boat, has produced fish to 5 pounds, with a decent number of shorts mixed in that you'll have to sort through. If you want a bigger average fish, work the deeper edge of the channel drop near the Coast Guard station side of the inlet on the last of the ebb — that's where the better-grade fluke have been holding tight to structure rather than sitting out on the open flat.

Bluefish have started showing more consistently inside the inlet itself, chopping up spearing and small bunker on the surface during the morning outgoing. Nothing like the bunker blitzes happening up the coast toward the city, but if you're out there at first light with a metal Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster, you can find a few slammers cutting through bait pods right off the rocks before the sun gets too high. It's a nice bonus fish if you're already out there for bass or working into a fluke morning.

Porgies and blackfish are still a canal-and-bridge story. The rock piles under Ponquogue and the structure heading toward the Shinnecock Canal locks are holding good numbers of porgies on sandworms and clam, fished on a simple high-low rig right on bottom during slack tide when the current isn't ripping them off the spot. Blackfish season's still off out here, but I've seen a few guys picking through legal-sized porgies mixed with some decent-sized weakfish drifting the mouth of the canal on the tail end of the outgoing — worth a look if you're heading toward the Peconic side anyway.

Looking ahead, the neap tide is going to hold through midweek, which means softer current and longer bite windows both at the inlet and the bridge — good news for anyone who can only get out for a few hours instead of chasing the peak of a hard tide. If the warm, calm pattern holds like it has, I'd expect the weakfish at Ponquogue to keep building through the week, and the inlet bass to stay locked into that midnight-to-3-a.m. window on the outgoing. If a front comes through and stirs up the bay, the fluke bite on the flats might get choppy for a day or two, but structure spots like the channel edge by the Coast Guard station should stay productive regardless. My plan this week is simple: eels at the jetty after midnight, bucktails at the bridge at dusk. That's where I'm putting my time, and that's where I'd send you too.
